blocks.body:
Modulo $q$ there are two natural families of "waves". The additive characters $n\mapsto e(an/q)$, where $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$, respect addition. The [[dirichlet-characters]] $\chi$ respect multiplication. A Gauss sum is the inner product of one with the other:
$$g(\chi)=\sum_{a\bmod q}\chi(a)\,e\Big(\frac aq\Big).$$
It is a sum of $\varphi(q)$ roots of unity, so a priori its size could be anything up to $\varphi(q)$. In fact, for primitive $\chi$, $|g(\chi)|$ is exactly $\sqrt q$, as if the terms were random signs. Gauss used the quadratic case to prove quadratic reciprocity, and Gauss sums reappear in the functional equation of the Dirichlet $L$-function of every primitive character.

blocks.title: Warm-up: p = 3 and p = 5
blocks.body:
Take $\chi$ to be the Legendre symbol $\left(\frac{\cdot}{p}\right)$, and write $\zeta=e(1/p)$.

For $p=3$: $g=\zeta-\zeta^2=2i\sin(2\pi/3)=i\sqrt3$.

For $p=5$: the squares mod $5$ are $1$ and $4$, so $g=\zeta+\zeta^4-\zeta^2-\zeta^3=2\cos\frac{2\pi}5-2\cos\frac{4\pi}5$. This is $\sqrt5$, as we will see in an example below.

In both cases $g^2=\pm p$, with sign $+$ for $p\equiv1\pmod 4$ and $-$ for $p\equiv3\pmod 4$. There is also a second description. The number of $x$ with $x^2\equiv a$ is $1+\left(\frac ap\right)$, so
$$\sum_{x\bmod p}e\Big(\frac{x^2}p\Big)=\sum_{a\bmod p}\Big(1+\Big(\frac ap\Big)\Big)e\Big(\frac ap\Big)=g,$$
because $\sum_a e(a/p)=0$. So the quadratic Gauss sum is also the sum of $e(x^2/p)$ over all $x$.

blocks.title: Gauss sum
blocks.body:
For a character $\chi$ mod $q$ and an integer $b$,
$$g(\chi,b)=\sum_{a\bmod q}\chi(a)\,e\Big(\frac{ab}q\Big),\qquad g(\chi)=g(\chi,1).$$
It measures how much the multiplicative character $\chi$ correlates with the additive character $a\mapsto e(ab/q)$.

blocks.title: Separating the variables
blocks.body: If $\gcd(b,q)=1$, then $g(\chi,b)=\overline\chi(b)\,g(\chi)$. If $\chi$ is primitive, this identity holds for every integer $b$, since then both sides vanish when $\gcd(b,q)>1$.

If $\gcd(b,q)=1$, substitute $a=b^{-1}c$, so that $c=ab$ runs over all residues as $a$ does. Then $g(\chi,b)=\sum_c\chi(b^{-1}c)e(c/q)=\overline\chi(b)g(\chi)$.

Now let $\chi$ be primitive and $d=\gcd(b,q)>1$, and put $q_1=q/d$, a proper divisor of $q$. Since $\chi$ is not induced from modulus $q_1$, the test in [[dirichlet-characters]] gives an integer $c\equiv1\pmod{q_1}$ with $\gcd(c,q)=1$ and $\chi(c)\ne1$. Write $b=db'$ and $c=1+q_1k$. Then $cb=b+qb'k\equiv b\pmod q$. Replacing $a$ by $ac$ permutes the residues mod $q$, so
$$g(\chi,b)=\sum_a\chi(ac)e\Big(\frac{acb}q\Big)=\chi(c)\sum_a\chi(a)e\Big(\frac{ab}q\Big)=\chi(c)\,g(\chi,b).$$
Since $\chi(c)\ne1$, $g(\chi,b)=0=\overline\chi(b)g(\chi)$.

blocks.title: Absolute value
blocks.body:
If $\chi$ is a primitive character mod $q$, then
$$|g(\chi)|^2 = q .$$

Compute $\Sigma=\sum_{b\bmod q}|g(\chi,b)|^2$ in two ways.

By the previous theorem, which holds for all $b$ because $\chi$ is primitive, $|g(\chi,b)|^2=|\chi(b)|^2|g(\chi)|^2$. Hence $\Sigma=\varphi(q)|g(\chi)|^2$.

Expanding the square instead,
$$\Sigma=\sum_{a_1,a_2}\chi(a_1)\overline{\chi(a_2)}\sum_b e\Big(\frac{b(a_1-a_2)}q\Big).$$
The inner sum is $q$ if $a_1\equiv a_2$ and $0$ otherwise. So $\Sigma=q\sum_a|\chi(a)|^2=q\varphi(q)$. Comparing gives $|g(\chi)|^2=q$.

blocks.title: Primitivity matters
blocks.body: For imprimitive characters the size can be very different. For the principal character, $g(\chi_0)=\sum_{\gcd(a,q)=1}e(a/q)$ is the sum of the primitive $q$-th roots of unity, which equals $\mu(q)$. So $g(\chi_0)=-1$ for $q$ prime, and $0$ for $q=4$. In general, if $\chi$ mod $q$ is induced by a primitive $\chi^*$ mod $d$, one can show $g(\chi)=\mu(q/d)\chi^*(q/d)g(\chi^*)$. This vanishes, for instance, whenever $q/d$ is not squarefree.

blocks.title: The quadratic Gauss sum
blocks.body:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $\chi=\left(\frac{\cdot}{p}\right)$. Then
$$g(\chi)^2=\Big(\frac{-1}{p}\Big)p=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\,p .$$
Gauss proved the sharper statement $g(\chi)=\sqrt p$ if $p\equiv1\pmod 4$ and $g(\chi)=i\sqrt p$ if $p\equiv3\pmod 4$. Determining this sign is genuinely harder, and Gauss reported that it took him years; we do not prove it here.

The character $\chi$ is real and primitive (every nonprincipal character mod a prime is primitive). So $|g|^2=p$. Also
$$\overline{g}=\sum_a\chi(a)e\Big(-\frac ap\Big)=g(\chi,-1)=\chi(-1)\,g,$$
using separation with $b=-1$ and $\overline\chi=\chi$. Hence $p=g\overline g=\chi(-1)g^2$, and $g^2=\chi(-1)p$. Finally, $\chi(-1)=\left(\frac{-1}p\right)=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}$ by Euler's criterion.

blocks.title: Quadratic reciprocity from Gauss sums
blocks.body:
Let $p\ne\ell$ be odd primes, $\chi=\left(\frac{\cdot}{p}\right)$, $g=g(\chi)$, and $p^*=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}p$, so that $g^2=p^*$. Work in the ring $\mathbb Z[\zeta]$, $\zeta=e(1/p)$, whose elements are integer polynomials in $\zeta$. Write $\alpha\equiv\beta\pmod\ell$ if $\alpha-\beta\in\ell\,\mathbb Z[\zeta]$.

Step 1. $$g^\ell=g\,(g^2)^{(\ell-1)/2}=g\,(p^*)^{(\ell-1)/2}\equiv\Big(\frac{p^*}{\ell}\Big)g\pmod\ell$$, by Euler's criterion for the integer $p^*$ modulo $\ell$.

Step 2. In any commutative ring, $(x+y)^\ell\equiv x^\ell+y^\ell\pmod\ell$, because the binomial coefficients $\binom\ell k$ with $0<k<\ell$ are divisible by $\ell$. Since $\chi(a)^\ell=\chi(a)$ ($\ell$ is odd),
$$g^\ell\equiv\sum_a\chi(a)\zeta^{a\ell}=g(\chi,\ell)=\chi(\ell)\,g\pmod\ell .$$
Step 3. So $\big(\frac{p^*}\ell\big)g\equiv\big(\frac\ell p\big)g$. Multiply by $g$: $\big(\frac{p^*}\ell\big)p^*\equiv\big(\frac\ell p\big)p^*\pmod\ell$. Both sides are integers, and $1,\zeta,\dots,\zeta^{p-2}$ is a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $\mathbb Z[\zeta]$ (because the minimal polynomial $1+x+\cdots+x^{p-1}$ of $\zeta$ is monic of degree $p-1$; see [[cyclotomic]]). So an integer lies in $\ell\mathbb Z[\zeta]$ only if it is divisible by $\ell$ in $\mathbb Z$. As $\ell\nmid p^*$, we get $\big(\frac{p^*}\ell\big)\equiv\big(\frac\ell p\big)\pmod\ell$. Two signs that agree mod $\ell\ge3$ are equal.

Step 4. $\big(\frac{p^*}\ell\big)=\big(\frac{-1}\ell\big)^{(p-1)/2}\big(\frac p\ell\big)=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}2\cdot\frac{\ell-1}2}\big(\frac p\ell\big)$. Together with step 3, this is the law of quadratic reciprocity ([[quadratic-residues]]).

blocks.title: The regular pentagon
blocks.body: Use the Gauss sum mod $5$ to show $\cos\frac{2\pi}5=\frac{\sqrt5-1}4$.
blocks.solution:
Let $\zeta=e(1/5)$, $u=\zeta+\zeta^4=2\cos\frac{2\pi}5$ and $v=\zeta^2+\zeta^3=2\cos\frac{4\pi}5$. Since $1+\zeta+\zeta^2+\zeta^3+\zeta^4=0$, we have $u+v=-1$. The quadratic Gauss sum is $g=u-v$. Since $5\equiv1\pmod4$, the theorem gives $g^2=5$. And $u>0>v$, because $\frac{2\pi}5<\frac\pi2<\frac{4\pi}5$, so $g=u-v>0$ and $g=\sqrt5$. Solving $u+v=-1$, $u-v=\sqrt5$ gives $u=\frac{\sqrt5-1}2$, that is, $\cos\frac{2\pi}5=\frac{\sqrt5-1}4$.

The general principle is that $\sqrt{p^*}$ always lies in the field generated by the $p$-th roots of unity.

blocks.title: A complex character
blocks.body: Let $\chi$ be the character mod $5$ with $\chi(2)=i$. Compute $g(\chi)$, check $|g(\chi)|^2=5$, and verify $g(\chi)g(\overline\chi)=\chi(-1)\cdot5$.
blocks.solution:
From $2^1=2$, $2^2=4$, $2^3=3$ we get $\chi(1)=1$, $\chi(2)=i$, $\chi(4)=-1$, $\chi(3)=-i$. So
$$g(\chi)=\zeta+i\zeta^2-i\zeta^3-\zeta^4=(\zeta-\zeta^4)+i(\zeta^2-\zeta^3)=2i\sin\tfrac{2\pi}5-2\sin\tfrac{4\pi}5 .$$
Numerically this is $-1.17557+1.90211\,i$, and $1.17557^2+1.90211^2=5.0000$.

For the second identity, $g(\overline\chi)=\overline{g(\chi,-1)}=\overline{\chi(-1)g(\chi)}$ (separate the variables with $b=-1$), so $g(\chi)g(\overline\chi)=\overline{\chi(-1)}|g(\chi)|^2=\chi(-1)\cdot5$. Here $\chi(-1)=\chi(4)=-1$, so the product is $-5$. The same computation gives $g(\chi)g(\overline\chi)=\chi(-1)q$ for every primitive $\chi$ mod $q$.

blocks.title: Characters as combinations of additive waves
blocks.body:
Show that if $\chi$ is primitive mod $q$, then for every integer $n$
$$\chi(n)=\frac1{g(\overline\chi)}\sum_{a\bmod q}\overline\chi(a)\,e\Big(\frac{an}q\Big).$$
Why is this useful?
blocks.solution:
$\overline\chi$ is also primitive, so separation holds for all $n$: $g(\overline\chi,n)=\overline{\overline\chi}(n)g(\overline\chi)=\chi(n)g(\overline\chi)$. Since $g(\overline\chi)\ne0$ (its absolute value is $\sqrt q$), divide by it.

This is the finite Fourier expansion of $\chi$. The nonzero coefficients, those with $\gcd(a,q)=1$, all have the same size, $1/\sqrt q$. It turns any sum $\sum_n c_n\chi(n)$ into a combination of exponential sums $\sum_n c_ne(an/q)$. This is how the multiplicative [[large-sieve]] is derived from the additive one, and how the Pólya–Vinogradov inequality $\sum_{n\le N}\chi(n)\ll\sqrt q\log q$ is proved.

blocks.body:
- $|g(\chi)|=\sqrt q$ needs $\chi$ primitive. For $\chi_0$ mod a prime, $g=-1$; for imprimitive characters $g$ can vanish.
- $g^2=\left(\frac{-1}p\right)p$ is for the quadratic character mod an odd prime. Mod $2$ there is no nontrivial character at all.
- From $g^2=p^*$ alone you cannot tell $g$ from $-g$. The sign is a separate and harder theorem.
- Separation $g(\chi,b)=\overline\chi(b)g(\chi)$ for $\gcd(b,q)>1$ uses primitivity in an essential way.
- Normalisations vary: some books use $e(-a/q)$ or put $\overline\chi$ in the definition, which changes $g$ by $\chi(-1)$ or by complex conjugation.

For primitive $\chi$ mod $q$, the completed $L$-function $\Lambda(s,\chi)=(q/\pi)^{(s+\kappa)/2}\Gamma\big(\frac{s+\kappa}2\big)L(s,\chi)$, with $\kappa=0$ for even and $\kappa=1$ for odd $\chi$, satisfies $\Lambda(s,\chi)=\varepsilon(\chi)\Lambda(1-s,\overline\chi)$ with root number $\varepsilon(\chi)=g(\chi)/(i^\kappa\sqrt q)$, a complex number of absolute value $1$ ([[l-functions]]). The expansion of $\chi$ in additive characters is the bridge to the [[large-sieve]] and to [[exponential-sums]]. Products of Gauss sums give Jacobi sums, $J(\chi,\psi)=g(\chi)g(\psi)/g(\chi\psi)$ when $\chi\psi$ is nontrivial. These are the key to [[cubic-characters]] and cubic reciprocity, and to counting points on curves over [[finite-fields]].

1. Compute the quadratic Gauss sum mod $7$ directly, and check that it equals $i\sqrt7$.
2. Show that $g(\chi_0)=\mu(q)$ for the principal character mod $q$. (Use Möbius inversion on $\sum_{d\mid\gcd(a,q)}\mu(d)$.)
3. For an odd prime $p$ and $p\nmid a$, show that $\big|\sum_{x\bmod p}e(ax^2/p)\big|=\sqrt p$.
4. Let $\chi,\psi$ be nontrivial characters mod a prime $p$ with $\chi\psi$ nontrivial. Prove $g(\chi)g(\psi)=J(\chi,\psi)g(\chi\psi)$, where $J(\chi,\psi)=\sum_{a}\chi(a)\psi(1-a)$, and deduce $|J(\chi,\psi)|=\sqrt p$.
